PC: Obtain a history from a distraught family member.
Review the medical record, including the vital signs and respiratory logs, and laboratory evaluations.
No pupillary responses to bright light
No response to noxious stimuli at the temporal-mandibular joint or supraorbital nerve
No cough response to tracheal suctioning (the nurse already performed this and there was no response)
No motor response to noxious stimuli in all 4 limbs (spinally mediated reflexes are permissible)
MK: Irreversible coma with a known cause
No severe electrolyte, acid-base, or endocrine abnormality
Ideally, the physicians should recognize the patient does not yet meet brain death criteria, because she is breathing over the ventilator.
No apnea test is indicated because the patient is breathing over the ventilator.
SBP: Call a code if necessary and appropriate.
The physicians would respect the family member’s wishes and would not code the patient.
ICS: Empathy: Unless you have been in the situation, it can be difficult to imagine a family member undergoing a brain death examination. The family member feels a complete loss of control, and is looking to you to provide answers. You may feel you are being attacked or blamed, but realize this is part of a normal grieving process. Tell the family member that you realize this is an extremely difficult situation.
Introductions: Introduce yourself, and shake hands with the family member. Ask what is his or her relationship with the patient. Afterwards, refer to the patient as “your mother.”
Comfort: Pull up a chair, and invite the family member to have a seat. This will make the family member more comfortable and give you more room to complete your examination.

Reassurance: You can’t reassure the family member that everything will be alright. You can, however, reassure the family member that you will conduct a thorough examination and answer all questions to the best of your abilities. This is the hardest thing for medical students, because you want to give hope and offer treatment or a cure. However, at this moment, the family member needs facts and guidance through this process.

Using lay terminology: Ensure that you use lay terminology. The family member is overwhelmed with grief and may have difficulty comprehending everything that is happening. Avoiding medical jargon can help.
The physicians should inform the family member that the prognosis is extremely poor.
PROF: The treating physician serves as the patient’s advocate; therefore, does not broach the subject of organ donation.
